seo.title: Karmic tail 9 6 15 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 6 15 compatibility in the destiny matrix: the Hermit at the entry, the Lovers in the middle and the Devil as the main task, with a worked example.

title: Karmic tail 9-6-15 in compatibility: the Hermit, the Lovers and the Devil
short: The most common couple tail has strange arithmetic: the Hermit plus the Lovers make exactly the Devil, 9 + 6 = 15, with no reduction at all. Solitude for two, added to love, turns into attachment, and that is the whole plot of the 9-6-15 tail. The couple enters the task with a shared wish to shut the world out together, goes through it by love and by choosing each other day after day, and the main task is the Devil: not to let care, habit and the fear of loss become a chain that binds the two only to each other.

sections.h2: How the 9-6-15 tail is worked out in compatibility: an example with two dates
paragraphs: Each point of a couple’s matrix is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple’s tail is not taken from one date or guessed from the partners’ numbers: point is added to point.
An example: 05.07.1975 and 14.08.1975. The first date has the personal tail 12-19-7, the second 15-5-8. Add them point by point:

The couple’s middle is added up too, not derived from the ends: 19 + 5. But in this triple it also agrees with the ends: 9 + 15 = 24 → 6. And the first two cards add up to the third: 9 + 6 = 15. In the 9-6-15 tail each number comes out of the other two.

This couple’s centre is 5 + 7 = 12, the Hanged Man, and “The couple’s values” holds 9: the Hermit a second time. And one more detail we will come back to: on the “What to create together” point the couple has 7 + 8 = 15, the same Devil.

The 9-6-15 tail is the most frequent of the 97 couple tails: it falls to 4.627% of couples, about one in 22. It is built from only six combinations of personal tails. The three most common are 15-20-5 with 21-4-10 (37% of such couples), 12-19-7 with 15-5-8, as in the example (37%), and 18-9-9 with 9-15-6 (13%).

As a personal tail 9-6-15 never occurs: this triple is not among the 26 personal tails. In one person’s chart the Devil in the karmic task always comes with the Empress in the centre and the Moon at the entry — that is the tail 18-6-15. The sequence “Hermit, Lovers, Devil” exists only in a couple.

sections.h2: Old World Landowners: the couple who had no evil spirit
paragraphs: In 1835 Gogol opened his collection Mirgorod with a story about two old people, Afanasy Ivanovich and Pulkheria Ivanovna Tovstogub. The narrator himself tells us which myth to hold it against: “If I were a painter and wished to put Philemon and Baucis on canvas, I would never choose any other model but them” (here and below, Gogol’s words are in our translation).

The story’s first paragraph reads almost like a description of this tail’s entry. The narrator likes “to step down for a minute into the sphere of that uncommonly secluded life, where not a single wish flies over the palisade that surrounds the little yard”. And further: the owners’ life is “so quiet, so quiet, that for a minute one forgets oneself and thinks that passions, desires and the restless offspring of the evil spirit that trouble the world do not exist at all”.

That sentence holds the whole riddle of the 9-6-15 tail. The couple builds its world so that there is no evil spirit in it, and the couple’s main task turns out to be the Devil himself. Gogol shows how this comes about. Between the two old people there are no betrayals and no scenes; nobody slams a door. The Devil here does not break down the gate — he grows inside the palisade, out of tenderness, care and habit.
Read beside the three cards, the story falls into the points of the tail.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the entry: keeping the world beyond the palisade
paragraphs: “Entry to the task” is what the couple wants together: its shared wishes and agreements. Lisovskaya also calls this point the point of common language, and with it the point of resistance: a wish may not match reality, and then the couple runs up against its own dream.

The common language of the old-world landowners can be heard from the first page. They speak to each other only in the formal “you”, the Russian vy: “Was it you who pushed the seat of the chair through, Afanasy Ivanovich?” — “Never mind, don’t be cross, Pulkheria Ivanovna: it was me.” Their day is marked out by one and the same question: “Well, Pulkheria Ivanovna, perhaps it’s time for a little bite of something?” It is the language of two people who hardly need a third. Even in the closest intimacy they keep that small formal vy — a distance nobody ever breaks.

In a couple today with this entry everything looks different, yet it is recognisable at once. The two leave a noisy party first, and in the taxi they feel better than they did all evening. They talk about plans once everything is already decided. A Friday evening without guests is not boredom but a reward. The Hermit at the entry is a wish they have shared since their first meetings: a corner of their own, a pace of their own, words of their own.

The resistance grows from the same place. Everything that comes from outside — friends, family, one partner’s new interest, an offer to move — is first tested for one thing: will it disturb the quiet? The wish “let them leave us alone” quietly becomes a rule, and the rule becomes a fence that no wish flies over. Not even their own.

The numbers add a detail. In 86% of couples with the 9-6-15 tail neither partner has the Hermit in their personal tail. On their own they do not carry this card in the tail: the Hermit appears only when the two are added together. The same point M is also the end of the couple’s relationship line, “Common language”. And in “The couple’s values” the Hermit stands for 63.9% of such couples: a quiet world for two is for them not only the entry but also what the union exists for.

Wen writes of the Hermit: “He is neutral in the war between good and evil. He has transcended that war and has found peace.” In Gogol peace is arranged differently. Nobody transcended the war; it was left beyond the palisade. Hence the tail’s task: what was not let in at the gate does not vanish, it looks for a way inside.

sections.h2: The Lovers in the middle: a choice that was forgotten
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the “Middle of the task” has no meaning of its own — it adds to the main task. In our reading the middle shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task: what it does and what it goes through. In the 9-6-15 tail this road is laid by love.

Gogol mentions in passing how the quiet house began. Afanasy Ivanovich married at thirty, “when he was a fine young fellow and wore an embroidered waistcoat; he even carried off, quite deftly, Pulkheria Ivanovna, whom her relatives did not want to give him”. There they are, the Lovers: a choice against the family’s will, an elopement, a decision of two. And right after: “but even of this he remembered very little now, at least he never spoke of it”.

That is the whole middle of the tail. Love in such a couple is not a feeling to be talked about but a thing to be done: someone has saved “dumplings with berries” for the other on purpose, someone remembers which pies the other likes. “One could not look without sympathy at their mutual love,” writes Gogol. But the choice where it all began has long since become a given. Nobody repeats it — it is simply there, like the walls of the house.

Wen notes of the Lovers: “Overall, there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning.” The middle of the 9-6-15 tail decides what becomes of that paradise later. The Lovers stand here between the Hermit and the Devil and are made of them: 9 + 15 = 24 → 6. This couple’s love is made of two substances — solitude and attachment. While the choice of each other is made again, love keeps the solitude open. When the choice is forgotten, only attachment is left.

In a couple today the middle shows in small things. One partner makes decisions “for both of us” because it is quicker. The other stops asking whether the first wants the same — it is obvious anyway. The relationship is gradually measured against the picture of “how it used to be with us”, and any difference from it is frightening. Among the Lovers’ tasks in a couple Lisovskaya names perfectionism and idealising the relationship, and insecurity that breeds jealousy and control. In the 9-6-15 tail none of this sounds like a scene; it sounds like a quiet wish that nothing should change.

sections.h2: The Devil as the main task: “grew attached through habit”
paragraphs: The “Main task” is the couple’s chief problem and trial, and it is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what has to be learned. For Lisovskaya the Devil in this place means dependence and the wish to possess, attempts to hold on to the partner, silence about one’s own wishes, fear and hopelessness. Her final thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple: nobody belongs to anybody.

Gogol gives this Devil an exact definition — about a cat, as it happens: “One cannot say that Pulkheria Ivanovna loved her too much; she had simply grown attached to her, having grown used to always seeing her.” Grown attached through habit: not passion and not vice, but the habit of seeing someone nearby. And of the old couple themselves we are told that “all their attachment was concentrated on themselves”. Attachment has nowhere to flow beyond the palisade, and all of it goes into each other.
Then the story shows how this attachment works, in scenes almost any couple will recognise.

At night Afanasy Ivanovich groans. “Why are you groaning?” — “Oh, as if my belly aches a little.” — “Wouldn’t it be better to eat something?” He eats a small plateful and says: “Now it’s as if it has become easier.” The remedy for unease is a little more of what causes the unease. Wen describes the Devil as a “preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification”. In a couple it looks like this: dinner instead of a conversation, a present instead of the question “what’s wrong?”, one more cosy evening instead of a change.

A guest at their house “was on no account let go the same day: he absolutely had to stay the night”. The hospitality is real and warm, and still the guest is not let go. Care inside such a couple is built the same way: it is sincere, but it has no door to the outside.

And when Afanasy Ivanovich feels like joking, he asks: “Well, Pulkheria Ivanovna, what if our house suddenly caught fire, where would we go?” Or he announces that he is off to the war. She gets cross: “I know he’s joking, and yet it’s unpleasant to hear… sometimes you listen and listen, and you get frightened.” This couple’s merriest game is to imagine that the shelter is gone or that one of them leaves. Their fear of loss lives not in quarrels but in jokes.

And the strongest scene. Pulkheria Ivanovna, sure that she will soon die, regrets only one thing: “I regret that I don’t know whom to leave you to, who will look after you when I die. You are like a little child.” She arranges everything so “that after her Afanasy Ivanovich should not notice her absence”. This is love — and it is also a chain: the care was so complete that the other forgot how to live on his own. Lisovskaya has a formula for such a union: one partner leads the other from the plus into the minus. In Gogol nobody leads anyone anywhere. The two simply did everything for each other for many years.
That is why the Devil of the 9-6-15 tail is so hard to recognise. He does not look like evil. He looks like a home that is warm and well fed, where someone is always close by.

sections.h2: The evidence in the numbers: the Devil is added up by the two
paragraphs: The numbers of this tail say the same thing as Gogol, only more briefly.

The first piece of evidence is already familiar: 9 + 6 = 15. The Hermit and the Lovers give the Devil without any reduction. A quiet world for two plus love equals attachment. This is not mysticism but the structure of the triple: the main task in it literally adds up from the entry and the middle.

The second piece of evidence is where the fifteen in the main task comes from. The couple’s main task is the sum of the two personal karmic tasks. In couples with the 9-6-15 tail these are always two small numbers that make 15 directly: 7 + 8, 5 + 10, 4 + 11 or 6 + 9. Neither partner has the Devil in their karmic task — he appears only in the sum. And in 13.5% of such couples the personal tasks are 6 and 9: one has the Lovers, the other the Hermit, and together they make the Devil again.

The third piece of evidence is where the Devil does appear. In 99.4% of couples with the 9-6-15 tail the fifteen stands in the personal tail of exactly one partner and never in both: almost always at the personal entry of the tail (86%), less often in its middle. This does not make him or her the “carrier” of the Devil. The fifteen reaches the couple’s main task not from there, but from the sum of two tasks in which neither has a fifteen.

The fourth is what the partners lack. In 86% of couples neither of the two has a nine or a six in their personal tail. The Hermit and the Lovers belong to the couple itself: they are not in the partners’ tails taken one by one.

Together the clues add up to one thought. Neither of the two brought this tail ready-made. The Hermit and the Lovers appear only in the sum of two charts, and the Devil comes from adding two tasks. Nobody forged this couple’s chain in advance — the two weave it themselves, day after day.

sections.h2: Waite and Papus: the Devil under whom two are bound only to each other
paragraphs: Waite describes his Devil card like this: in front of the altar there is a ring, and from it two chains run to the necks of a male and a female figure. “Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life,” he writes. And he adds at once that “he who is exalted above them is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman”.

Another passage matters more — in the first part of the book, where Waite goes through old designs of the card. On eighteenth-century decks two small demons are tied to the pedestal. In Papus’s book Le Tarot divinatoire, Waite writes, the demons were replaced by “naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other”. And he adds: “The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism.”

For the 9-6-15 tail this is the key line. Two people are bound not to a master and not to an altar, but only to each other — that is this couple’s Devil. There is no master: no one to overthrow and no one to run from. The two hold the chain themselves, and only they can take it off.

Yoked means “under one yoke, in one harness”, and in Waite the word sounds almost domestic. Max Vasmer writes of the Russian word for spouse, suprug: in Old Russian suprug meant “spouse”, “married couple, husband and wife” and “team of harnessed animals”; the word comes from prjagu, “I harness”, and is built the same way as Latin coniux (hence English “conjugal”) and Greek σύζυγος. Spouses are literally those harnessed together. Papus’s Devil is the shadow of the word “spouses” itself: the same harness, only with no cart and no road.

Waite even refuses to see the Hermit as a recluse. The card, he says, “is understood quite incorrectly when it is connected with the idea of occult isolation, as the protection of personal magnetism against admixture”, and he calls this one of the “frivolous renderings”. A couple at the 9-6-15 entry risks reading its Hermit in exactly that way — as a fence against strangers. In Waite the Hermit holds up his lantern on a height, like a beacon that says: “where I am, you also may be.”

Gogol opens the turning point by saying that the event “came from the most trifling occasion”. Beyond the garden, in a dense wood, live wild cats. For a long time they sniff at Pulkheria Ivanovna’s little cat through a hole under the barn and “at last lured her away, as a detachment of soldiers lures a silly peasant girl”. A few days later the cat comes back thin, eats greedily — and leaves again. “The ungrateful creature had evidently grown too used to the predatory cats, or had picked up the romantic rule that poverty with love is better than a palace, and the cats were as poor as church mice; be that as it may, she jumped out of the window.”

Gogol is mocking here, but the scene is precisely built. The cat repeats what Afanasy Ivanovich once did himself: she leaves a well-fed house for love. The household had grown attached to the cat, but the cat herself was not attached — and she left when she wished. And the mistress reads it like this: “That was my death that came for me!”

In a closed world any departure sounds like the end of the world. In his list of divinatory meanings for the Devil Waite names “fatality; that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”, and among the reversed ones “evil fatality, weakness, pettiness, blindness”. Pulkheria Ivanovna submits to the sign. A few years later Afanasy Ivanovich will submit in the same way, when in the quiet garden he seems to hear a voice calling his name: “he submitted with the will of an obedient child”.

The 9-6-15 tail says nothing about death — anyone’s. The cat scene matters for something else: this is how a closed world reads another’s freedom. If one of the two goes out for an evening with friends, to a course, into a venture of their own, a couple in the minus of this tail may feel it as a small end of the world. The task is to see in leaving not a verdict but freedom, without which coming back means nothing.

sections.h2: “Passion or habit?”: Gogol’s question and the tail’s answer
paragraphs: After Pulkheria Ivanovna’s death the narrator recalls a young man who was in love “tenderly, passionately, madly”. His beloved died, his despair was such that his family never let him out of their sight, and a year later the narrator sees him in a crowded hall playing cards, with a pretty young wife standing behind his chair. Five years on, Afanasy Ivanovich weeps “like a stream” over a dish that reminded him of the dead woman. Gogol asks: “Which then is stronger over us: passion or habit?” And he answers: “all our passions seemed childish” to him “against this long, slow, almost insensible habit”.
A few years earlier Pushkin had said of another landowning couple: “Habit is given us from above: it is a substitute for happiness.”

The 9-6-15 tail has its own answer to Gogol’s question. Passion and choice are the Lovers in the middle. Habit and attachment are the Devil in the main task. Gogol sets them against each other, while the tail puts them on one line: the Lovers are the road, the Devil is the task. The couple does not need to choose between them. It needs habit to remain a choice. Attachment that two people choose anew each day is no longer a chain but a harness: it pulls them both the same way.

sections.h2: The centre of a 9-6-15 couple: the Hanged Man, or a World no single person has
paragraphs: The centre of a couple’s matrix is its atmosphere, what is between the two and not on show. In couples with the 9-6-15 tail the centre is almost always one of two cards: 12, the Hanged Man, in 62.2%, and 21, the World, in 37.2%. The remaining 0.6% have the Empress.

Waite’s Hanged Man is “life in suspension, but life and not death”, and his face “expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”. This is exactly Gogol’s atmosphere, where all the old adventures “gave way to a quiet and secluded life, to those dozing and yet somehow harmonious reveries”. In the plus: depth, slow time, the ability to look at the world from a point of one’s own. In the minus: life on pause, where everything important is put off till later. Wen sees in the Hanged Man’s crossed legs “the balance between dominion and slavery” — the very line along which this couple’s Devil runs.

The World in the centre is a finding of a special kind. In the centre of a personal matrix 21 never occurs, for any date: such an atmosphere exists only in a couple. In these couples the personal centres are 10 and 11, the Wheel of Fortune and Strength, and a whole world appears only in their sum. The World is completion and fullness, and in Waite’s reversed list it is “inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence”. For a 9-6-15 couple these are two faces of one home: a world that has everything, and a world in which nothing moves any more.

In “The couple’s values” such couples have either the Hermit (63.9%) or the Moon (36.1%). Waite’s Moon is “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit” and “the fears of the natural mind”. In our reading, for couples with the Moon in their values the shared world also rests on imagination: on forebodings, signs and private meanings of their own. In Gogol these are the cat taken for a messenger and the voice in the garden.

sections.h2: What the 9-6-15 tail looks like in a couple’s life
paragraphs: In the plus this is a couple whose company is calming. It is good to be silent with them; people come to them to rest, like Gogol’s narrator, whose “soul took on a wonderfully pleasant and calm state” at their porch. The two understand each other from half a word, talk deep into the night, keep their word and keep their quarrels at home. Their love shows not in declarations but in deeds.
In the minus the same tail can be recognised by its scenes:

ul: **The evening that cannot be cancelled.** The couple has its ritual, and any invitation from outside is felt as an attack on it. One partner sometimes wants to go but does not: the other will say “of course, go” — and fall silent for the evening.
**Care instead of a conversation.** One feels bad; the other cooks, buys, arranges. The question “what happened?” never gets asked, because dinner is already on the table.

**The joke about leaving.** “One of these days I’ll leave you and join a monastery” — both laugh, and then the whole evening is heavy. The fear of loss hides in play, as with Afanasy Ivanovich’s fire and war.
**The wish that goes unspoken.** One wants to change jobs, to study, to go away for a month — and stays silent, because it threatens the quiet. The wish does not disappear; it piles up.

**Indispensability.** One does everything for the other: papers, phone calls, food, dealings with relatives. This is love, but after a few years the other can no longer manage without it — “you are like a little child”.

paragraphs: These scenes show how the tail’s cards work together. The Hermit and the Devil give silence: problems and wishes pile up without words. The Lovers and the Devil give a love that wants to hold on. The Hermit and the Lovers give a world for two, and all three together give a world that is hard to leave even for an evening.

sections.h2: What changes the story: a gate in the palisade
paragraphs: The task of the 9-6-15 tail is not to destroy the shared world. This couple needs its palisade: without a corner of its own it suffers. The task is to put a gate in it.

ul: **Each has a time and place of their own.** Among the Hermit’s pluses in a couple Lisovskaya names exactly this: each partner has a time for solitude. Solitude apart does not threaten what is shared; it airs it.

**A wish said aloud, and before it turns into a grievance.** Her own advice for the fifteenth energy: admit one’s secret wishes and talk about them. The rule is simple: if one wants something that will “disturb the quiet”, say so first.
**Make the choice again.** Not “but we’re together” but “I choose you” — in words, in questions, in small decisions. Ask rather than guess for the other.

**Care in a way that keeps the other capable.** Do not do for the other what they can do themselves; show where the keys are. The phrase “you are like a little child” is a good marker: once it starts to fit, care has become a chain.
**Turn the joke about loss into a conversation.** Say plainly what each is really afraid of, without fires and wars.

**Let go.** The guest when he wants to leave; each other for an evening, a course, a venture of one’s own. Pulkheria Ivanovna’s cat is the test: in this couple’s home freedom should not sound like disaster.

paragraphs: Waite leaves this card a way out right in its description: the one who holds the chain “is not to be their master for ever”. Wen writes that the reversed Devil means “the removal of bondage”. For a 9-6-15 couple the chains and the master are the two of them, and so they remove them themselves.
If attachment in a couple turns into control, prohibitions and fear, this is no longer a task for reading cards but a reason to see a family psychologist.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 9-6-15 tail: Philemon and Baucis
paragraphs: Gogol called his old couple Philemon and Baucis, and it is worth opening Ovid to see how the two couples differ. In the eighth book of the Metamorphoses Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travellers, knock at doors: “a thousand homes they approached, asking for rest; a thousand homes were shut against them by bolts; one took them in” (mille domos clausere serae; tamen una recepit — here and below our translation). The one that took them in was the house of a poor old couple.

Of the owners it is said: “it makes no difference whether you look there for masters or for servants: the whole household is two, and the same two give orders and obey” (tota domus duo sunt, idem parentque iubentque). This is what the Devil lacks: master and slave. In the house of Philemon and Baucis nobody is master over the other.

The two couples share the same Hermit — a small house far from everyone. The same Lovers — love for a whole life. Only the Devil differs. In Ovid the door opens to strangers when a thousand others are locked; in Gogol the guest is not let go. In Ovid nobody is anybody’s master; in Gogol one becomes the other’s nanny. At the end Philemon asks: “let the same hour take us both” (auferat hora duos eadem). The gods turn the old couple into two trees, and the local people still point out “neighbouring trunks from a twin body” (de gemino vicinos corpore truncos). Two trunks side by side, not one.

This is the strong version of the 9-6-15 tail. Not less closeness, but a door in it. Not one body for two, but two trunks growing side by side. Lisovskaya describes the Devil in a couple in the plus as well: passion, accepting each other’s dark sides and forgiving mistakes, open talk about desires, powerful support, attachment in the good sense; sometimes the union helps one leave earlier destructive relationships. In the example of 05.07.1975 and 14.08.1975 the Devil also stands on the “What to create together” point, which is read only in the plus. On this point, Lisovskaya says, fifteen very often means breaking free of dependence. In our reading this is the tail’s best answer: the Devil the couple wove itself, it also turns into freedom.

sections.h2: 9-6-15 and 9-15-6: the same numbers in another order
paragraphs: The same numbers give one more couple tail, 9-15-6, in 1.217% of couples; their centre is the Hanged Man in 77.8% and the World in 22.2%. There the Devil stands in the middle and the Lovers in the main task: the couple travels through attachment, and what it has to learn is love and choice themselves. In 9-6-15 it is the other way round: love is the road, and freedom within attachment is the task.

ul: **9 · The Hermit — “Entry to the task”.** What the couple wants together: quiet, a world of its own behind a fence, an unhurried pace, low-voiced talk. This wish is both the way into the task and the resistance to it: whatever comes from outside first looks like a nuisance.
**6 · The Lovers — “Middle of the task”.** What the couple goes through: love shown in deeds every day, and the choice of each other — made once, or made again and again.

**15 · The Devil — “Main task”.** What the couple has to learn: to tell closeness from ownership. Attachment with nowhere to flow but into each other becomes a chain, and only the two of them can take it off.

intro: A couple’s tail is not a forecast and not a verdict: it describes how the task is built, not what will happen. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the numbers themselves, what Waite and Benebell Wen saw in these cards, and why the best book about this tail was written by Gogol in 1835.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-6-15 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a tail of the couple’s matrix with the Hermit on the “Entry to the task”, the Lovers on the “Middle of the task” and the Devil on the “Main task”. The couple wants a quiet world for two, goes along the road through love and the choice of each other, and has to learn to tell closeness from ownership: not to let care and habit become a chain.

faq.q: Does 9-6-15 occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: Not as a karmic tail: this triple never occurs in a personal chart, and a person with the Devil in the karmic task always gets the tail 18-6-15. But the same three numbers do occur in a personal matrix as lines. As the relationship line (entry of relationships 9, under the heart 6, crossing of the lines 15) in 0.59% of dates, and as the money line (entry 9, middle 6, crossing 15) in 0.71% of dates. These are other points with other roles; a search for a “9 6 15 channel” may be about them.

faq.q: How can one check that a couple has the 9-6-15 tail?
faq.a: Work out both personal matrices and add the matching points of the tail, reducing sums over 22. For example, 05.07.1975 gives the personal tail 12-19-7 and 14.08.1975 gives 15-5-8; point by point that is 12 + 15 = 27 → 9, 19 + 5 = 24 → 6 and 7 + 8 = 15. The compatibility calculator does it automatically.

faq.q: Does the Devil in a couple’s tail mean infidelity or addiction?
faq.a: No. A card does not establish facts about people: infidelity, addiction, debts, anyone’s guilt. The Devil in the main task names a theme the couple has to learn on — attachment and ownership — and in the 9-6-15 tail this theme is usually a quiet one: care, habit, the fear of letting go.

faq.q: Whose Devil is it — his or hers?
faq.a: Nobody’s on their own. The couple’s main task is the sum of two personal karmic tasks, and in couples with the 9-6-15 tail neither partner has fifteen in the karmic task: 15 comes only from the addition, for example 7 + 8. The Devil does occur in one partner’s personal tail, but it does not reach the couple’s task from there.

faq.q: Why can a couple’s centre be 21 when no person has such a centre?
faq.a: A couple’s centre is the sum of two personal centres. A person never has 21 in the centre, but a couple can: in 37.2% of couples with the 9-6-15 tail the centre is the World, and it is made of the personal centres 10 and 11. It is an atmosphere neither of the two can bring alone: only the union creates it.

report: The Hermit plus the Lovers make exactly the Devil: 9 + 6 = 15, with no reduction. In the 9-6-15 tail this is not a coincidence but a plot. The couple enters the task with a shared wish for quiet and a world of its own, goes through it by love and by choosing each other, and the main task is the Devil: **not to let care, habit and the fear of loss become a chain** that binds the two only to each other.

report.h3: A house where the evil spirit seems not to exist

report: Gogol wrote the best description of this tail in 1835. Old World Landowners opens on an estate “where not a single wish flies over the palisade that surrounds the little yard”, and the owners’ life is “so quiet, so quiet, that for a minute one forgets oneself and thinks that passions, desires and the restless offspring of the evil spirit that trouble the world do not exist at all”. The couple builds a world with no evil spirit in it — and the Devil himself turns out to be its main task.

The Hermit on the “Entry to the task” is a wish shared since their first meetings: a corner of their own, a pace of their own, words of their own. Even in the closest intimacy Afanasy Ivanovich and Pulkheria Ivanovna never drop the formal form of address, and their day is marked out by one question — isn’t it time for a bite? It is the language of two who hardly need a third. But on this point the wish also turns into resistance: everything that comes from outside — friends, family, one partner’s new interest — is first tested for one thing: will it disturb the quiet?

The Lovers on the “Middle of the task” are a road laid by love. Long ago Afanasy Ivanovich “carried off, quite deftly” a bride whom her relatives did not want to give him, “but even of this he remembered very little now”. Love in such a couple is not words but deeds: “dumplings with berries” saved on purpose, the pies the other likes. But the choice that began it all has long become a given. While it is made again, love keeps the solitude open. When it is forgotten, only attachment is left.

Gogol gives this Devil an exact definition — about a cat, as it happens: “One cannot say that Pulkheria Ivanovna loved her too much; she had simply grown attached to her, having grown used to always seeing her.” Not passion and not vice, but the habit of seeing someone nearby. Of the old couple themselves we are told that “all their attachment was concentrated on themselves”. Attachment has nowhere to flow beyond the palisade.

Then the story shows how this works. At night Afanasy Ivanovich groans, and there is one remedy — to eat another small plateful: “Now it’s as if it has become easier.” The remedy for unease is a little more of what causes it. A guest at their house “was on no account let go the same day”. The husband’s merriest joke is to ask where they would go if the house burned down, or to announce that he is off to the war: their fear of loss lives not in quarrels but in jokes. And Pulkheria Ivanovna, sure she will soon die, regrets only that she does not know whom to leave him to: he is “like a little child”. **The care was so complete that the other forgot how to live on his own.**

That is why this Devil is so hard to recognise: he looks like a warm, well-fed home where someone is always close by. In a couple today he looks like this: dinner instead of a conversation, a present instead of the question “what’s wrong?”, and the wish to go away for a month stays unspoken because it threatens the quiet.

Waite writes of the two chained to the Devil and adds that the one above them “is not to be their master for ever”. But this tail is caught most precisely elsewhere in his book. Waite notes that in Papus the man and the woman on this card are “yoked only to each other”, and congratulates the author on this improved symbolism. There is no master. No one to overthrow and no one to run from: the two hold the chain themselves.

Yoked means “in one harness”. In Max Vasmer’s dictionary the Old Russian suprug, the word for spouse, meant “spouse”, “married couple, husband and wife” and “team of harnessed animals”: it comes from prjagu, “I harness”, like Latin coniux and Greek σύζυγος. Spouses are literally those harnessed together. **This couple’s Devil is the shadow of the word “spouses” itself**: the same harness, only with no cart and no road.

The numbers say the same. The couple’s main task is the sum of two personal karmic tasks, and in couples with this tail neither partner has fifteen in the karmic task: the Devil appears only in the addition. Nobody brought him ready-made — the two weave him themselves, day after day.

In Gogol the turning point begins with the cat. Wild cats from the wood lured her away; she came back thin, ate her fill and jumped out of the window again, as if she had “picked up the romantic rule that poverty with love is better than a palace”. The cat repeated what Afanasy Ivanovich had once done himself: she left a well-fed house for love. And the mistress read it as a verdict: “That was my death that came for me!” **In a closed world any departure sounds like the end of the world.** The tail says nothing about death; the scene is about something else — how a closed world reads another’s freedom. An evening one of the two spends with friends, a course, a venture of their own may feel like a small catastrophe to a couple in the minus of this tail.
The task is not to destroy the shared world: without a corner of its own this couple suffers. The task is to put a gate in the palisade:

ul: each has a time and place for solitude;
a wish said aloud, and before it turns into a grievance;
the choice of each other made again: asking rather than guessing for the other;
care that keeps the other able to live on their own;
the joke about loss turned into a conversation about what each is really afraid of;
letting go — of the guest when he wants to leave, and of each other.

report: If attachment turns into control, prohibitions and fear, it is no longer a task for reading cards but a reason to see a family psychologist.

Gogol himself named the strong version of this tail — Philemon and Baucis. In Ovid it is said of their hut: “the whole household is two, and the same two give orders and obey”. No master, no slave. Their door opened to travellers when a thousand others were locked, and at the end the old couple became two trees — “neighbouring trunks from a twin body”. Not one body for two, but two trunks growing side by side. Attachment that two people choose anew each day is no longer a chain but a harness: it pulls them both the same way.
